1.ask: A contract holds an OLD value and a NEW value. The model keeps picking one at random. What fixes the extraction itself?
1.first: Spot 'no indication of which applies' — the output can only hold ONE value. Look for the choice that lets it hold both.

2.ask: Plain question: how does info actually travel between subagents in Claude's architecture?
2.first: Subagents are sealed boxes. Only one path exists — through the coordinator's prompt.

3.ask: Synthesis calls 18% (2022) vs 35% (2024) a contradiction. What's it missing, and who should hand it over?
3.first: The dates exist upstream but never reach synthesis. Prioritize the choice that carries dates forward.

4.ask: Angry customer wants a human — but the fix takes 10 seconds. Best reply?
4.first: Two facts collide: 'wants a person' + 'instantly fixable'. Find the option honoring BOTH.

5.ask: Tools run in the wrong order — enrichment before extraction. How do you GUARANTEE just the first step?
5.first: You need a guarantee for step 1 only. Beware anything that locks ALL steps, or that merely hopes.

6.ask: Half the job worked, half hit a system error. What do you tell the customer?
6.first: The agent HAS useful info. Rule out lying and infinite retries; look for honest partial delivery.

7.ask: One expensive analysis, two ideas to test separately. Which session move copies the past into two futures?

8.ask: The model INVENTS plausible values for fields the article never mentions. Cheapest targeted fix?
8.first: The model was never told 'empty is OK'. Permission-to-say-null beats new machinery.

9.ask: THREE different judgment inconsistencies at once. Which single fix teaches all three?
9.first: Count the problems: 3. Kill any option fixing only 1. Demonstration beats description.

10.ask: REVERSED question — which failure does retrying NOT help? (3 of these are retry-friendly.)
10.first: Retry = 'try again with feedback'. It can reshape output; it cannot create missing information.

11.ask: 8,000 lines across 15 files, limited context. Understand cache invalidation without drowning — how?
11.first: 'Managing context constraints' kills read-everything. 'Understand how it works' kills grep-only. Middle path: follow the architecture.

12.ask: One mushy do-anything tool → 35% garbage responses. What's the STRUCTURAL fix?
12.first: 'Free-text instruction parameter' is the disease. Anything that keeps that parameter is a bandage.

13.ask: The citation agent must link claims to sources. What's ENOUGH info — without shipping all 120K tokens?
13.first: 'Balance completeness and efficiency' — kill the two extremes first (names-only, ship-everything).

14.ask: Named session from last week, 3 other codebases used since. Which command returns EXACTLY there?
14.first: 'Most recent' ≠ 'the one you want'. She KNOWS the name — use the flag that takes a name.

15.ask: JSON is valid but fields come back EMPTY — the info exists, in varied layouts. Is this a skill gap or a luck gap?
15.first: The model can't RECOGNIZE the formats. Retrying re-rolls the same blindness; teaching fixes it.

16.ask: Paused agent + one tiny KNOWN change (2 renamed functions). Cheapest safe restart?
16.first: The change is small and known. Keep the 47-file context; patch the two facts.

17.ask: Valid session, 3 of 12 files changed overnight. What's efficient AND accurate?
17.first: 9 files unchanged → don't re-read them. 3 changed → don't ignore them. The answer literally names the 3.

18.ask: Crash at doc 12 of 28. Resume without redoing work — balancing fidelity against tokens?
18.first: 'Balance' is the graded word. Full log = max fidelity, max tokens. Find compact-but-faithful.

19.ask: Messy formats ($12 vs 12.00 vs '12 dollars'). Where should normalization live for max reliability?
19.first: Kill the cost-absurd options first (per-field calls, vote-of-5). Then: fix at the source vs downstream.

20.ask: Simple queries waste the full 4-agent pipeline — and the query mix keeps EVOLVING. What routing survives change?
20.first: 'Diverse and evolving' murders static rules and trained classifiers. Who adapts for free? The LLM already in the room.

21.ask: 97% accuracy overall. Before auto-approving anything, what must you check FIRST?
21.first: 'Overall' is the trap word. Averages hide a terrible segment.

22.ask: Definition check: in an agentic loop, WHO or WHAT picks the next tool?
22.first: 'Agentic' = the model steers, every turn. Anything pre-scripted or externally routed is a workflow, not an agent.

23.ask: Summarization keeps eating the source metadata. Where should metadata live so it CAN'T be eaten?
23.first: Prose can always be paraphrased away. A separate FIELD can't. Also: 'pass everything' = extremes die.

24.ask: Agent wastes retries on hopeless errors AND explains errors badly. One fix for BOTH symptoms?
24.first: Count the asks: wasted retries + bad explanations = 2. Some options fix one. One option fixes both.

25.ask: New MCP tools get ignored; each has a one-line description. How does the model pick tools at all?
25.first: The model reads descriptions to choose. Thin description = invisible tool.

26.ask: Tables, narrative, filings — all flattened to bullets, each losing its strength. Preserve them how?
26.first: Convert-to-prose and convert-to-JSON are the SAME mistake in opposite directions. A universal format is that mistake with extra steps.

27.ask: Context is rotting (generic answers), but the old findings MATTER for the new task. Keep what, shed what?
27.first: 'References typical patterns instead of the specific classes it discovered' = rot signal. Keep the knowledge, shed the bloat.

28.ask: SLA is 30 hours; a batch can take up to 24. What's the biggest safe gap between batch submissions?
28.first: Pure arithmetic: interval + 24 ≤ 30. Solve for interval.

29.ask: Sources detach from conclusions during multi-stage merging. Do you prevent it or repair it afterward?
29.first: Prevention (data that can't detach) beats archaeology (guessing later). Text tags get paraphrased away; fields don't.

30.ask: The coordinator narrates 'I'll ask the search agent…' — then nothing happens. Zero errors. What's missing?
30.first: Intent exists (it names the agents). Action never fires. Silent failure = missing tool permission, not missing knowledge.

31.ask: Intermittent 500 error, unknown cause, 200+ files. Plan everything first, or adapt as you learn?
31.first: 'Doesn't know which component' = you can't plan a path through fog. Each finding must steer the next step.

32.ask: 40-field payloads are flooding the conversation, with more coming. Keep what?
32.first: The task is a RETURN. Which fields does a return actually need? Keep exactly those.

33.ask: '3% failure rate' + 'guaranteed' + 'cannot be left to model discretion'. Prompt-family or code-family?
33.first: Guarantee = deterministic = code. Then pick the code option that ALSO handles the escalation requirement.

34.ask: Same info, different shape every time ('cotton blend' vs a list vs missing). What teaches ONE shape?
34.first: The model was never shown the target format. And beware: temp 0 = consistently random, not consistently right.

35.ask: The over-scripted subagent gives up instead of adapting. How much do you loosen the leash?
35.first: The script is the problem — but zero guidance loses quality control. Goldilocks: goals + quality criteria.

36.ask: The function gets renamed by wrapper modules. What does grepping the ORIGINAL name miss?
36.first: The stem hands you the trap: aliases. Enumerate every exposed name FIRST, then search each.

37.ask: The agent forgets the name given 3 turns ago. Where does 'memory' actually live in the Messages API?
37.first: The API is stateless. Memory = the messages array YOU resend. Two options describe features that don't exist.

38.ask: 8 files read, accuracy already dropping, 37 files to go. WHO should do the remaining reading?
38.first: The main context is precious real estate. Delegate the heavy reading; import only conclusions.

39.ask: Yesterday's deep analysis + two rival designs to explore. Same shape as Q7?
39.first: Twin question. 'Explore both in depth' + shared prior analysis = fork.

40.ask: 4 fixed property types; reality keeps inventing new ones (8% failures). Keep validation AND absorb novelty?
40.first: 'New types continue appearing' kills enum whack-a-mole. 'Keep validation' kills free-text.

41.ask: Synthesis either flattens disagreement into false confidence, or hedges everything. How do you PRESENT uncertainty?
41.first: Disagreement is CONTENT, not noise. Kill anything that deletes it (filters) or blends it (averaging).

42.ask: Every error says 'Operation failed'; the agent guesses wrong constantly. WHERE does knowledge of the error type live?
42.first: The TOOL knows why it failed. Make it say so — don't make the agent investigate or guess.

43.ask: Synthesis says 'no findings were provided'. Subagents are sealed — so whose job was delivery?
43.first: 'NO findings' ≠ 'truncated findings'. The courier is the coordinator.

44.ask: 12 sequential precedent analyses = 36 slow minutes. Parallelize while the coordinator can still SEE everything?
44.first: 'Preserve the coordinator's ability to monitor' kills every option where spawning happens below the coordinator.

45.ask: 80K tokens shipped to another agent… to summarize what the shipper ALREADY knows. Spot the absurdity?
45.first: 'The coordinator already has these findings in its context' — the transfer itself is the waste.

46.ask: A rich tool with a 4-word description loses to well-documented Grep every time. Coincidence?
46.first: The stem SHOWS you both descriptions side by side. The gap IS the bug.

47.ask: Refund needs a manager ($500+). What should travel WITH the escalation so no work gets repeated?
47.first: The agent already investigated. Escalation quality = how little the human must redo.

48.ask: Turn 48; customer asks about issue #1 from turn 5. What kind of storage survives 48 turns INTACT?
48.first: You'll need EXACT order IDs and amounts later. Whatever you keep must preserve those verbatim, for ALL issues.

49.ask: 'Explained my issue twice' + 'REAL PERSON NOW'. Honor it or negotiate?
49.first: Contrast with Q4: there the fix was instant. Here the agent knows NOTHING yet and they've been burned twice already.

50.ask: The human gets NO transcript. What's the minimum COMPLETE package?
50.first: Test each option: could a stranger act on it ALONE? Find the account? Know the cause? Know what to do?

51.ask: Edit can't find a unique anchor in repetitive code. Which tool combo doesn't NEED an anchor?
51.first: The stem says insert into the MIDDLE — kill the append-to-end option instantly. Then: fragile match vs bulletproof rewrite.

52.ask: 30 minutes in, the agent contradicts its own earlier findings. In-window memory is failing — store findings WHERE?
52.first: In-window memory degrades regardless of size. Durable memory = a FILE the agent re-reads.

53.ask: Which escalation trigger catches REAL need without false alarms?
53.first: Test each trigger against Q49's customer (zero tool calls, calm words, explicit demand): which one catches them?

54.ask: Pure spec recall: how do MCP tools report failures so the MODEL can react?
54.first: The model can only react to what lands in the conversation. Exceptions die inside the framework.

55.ask: 300 of 10,000 failed with INPUT-too-long. Cheapest correct repair?
55.first: Two instant kills: anything reprocessing all 10,000, and max_tokens (caps OUTPUT — the error is INPUT).

56.ask: 800+ files, multiple services; you need the AUTH architecture. Trace one thread, or fan out?
56.first: Auth is one FLOW crossing services. A flow is traced end-to-end; fragments lose the plot. (Debate question — fan-out is defensible.)

57.ask: Old tool data keeps leaking into answers EVEN AFTER fresh calls. Can stale context be out-instructed?
57.first: The stem already ran that experiment for you: fresh calls didn't fix it. Only ABSENCE fixes it.

58.ask: Mixed workload: 30-minute urgent alerts + don't-care archive. One processing lane or two?
58.first: A batch can take 24 HOURS. Any option that puts urgent reports in a batch is dead on arrival.

59.ask: Totals disagree; the cause could be OCR OR the model. Which side do you trust — or neither?
59.first: It's ACCOUNTING data. Any option that silently 'fixes' numbers = fabricating records. Surface the conflict; don't decide it.

60.ask: Errors LOOK valid (they pass the schema). You can review 20% — spend it where?
60.first: The failure mode is confidently-wrong FILLED fields. Empty fields are the honest ones. Random catches only 1 in 5.

1.A: Says: after extracting, run a pattern-matching checker that spots amendment contracts and sends them to a human.
1.B: Says: change the output shape so one field holds BOTH terms, each tagged with its effective date.
1.C: Says: before the model reads the contract, delete the superseded old terms.
1.D: Says: tell the model 'when terms conflict, always take the amendment version.'

2.A: Says: all agents read and write one shared memory store.
2.B: Says: the boss agent takes agent 1's answer and pastes it into agent 2's instructions.
2.C: Says: agents mail each other through a message-queue system.
2.D: Says: agents call each other directly, no middleman.

3.A: Says: make every finding carry its date as a data field, e.g. {value: '35%', as_of: 2024}.
3.B: Says: tell synthesis 'when numbers differ, trust the newest one.'
3.C: Says: automatically discard data older than a cutoff.
3.D: Says: restrict searching to the past 6 months so old data never appears.

4.A: Says: just process the refund right away without asking.
4.B: Says: hand them to a human immediately because they asked for one.
4.C: Says: ask more clarifying questions first.
4.D: Says: apologize, tell them it's fixable RIGHT NOW, and let THEM choose: fix now or talk to a person.

5.A: Says: lock the model to extract_metadata on EVERY request, forever.
5.B: Says: require 'some tool' each turn ('any') and hint the desired order in the prompt.
5.C: Says: list extract_metadata first in the tools array, hoping order = priority.
5.D: Says: force extract_metadata on call #1 only, then unlock (auto) for the following turns.

6.A: Says: give up and hand the whole case to a human.
6.B: Says: keep the customer waiting while retrying until the refund succeeds.
6.C: Says: share the good news (return approved, label sent), admit the refund error, offer retry-or-human.
6.D: Says: tell them the refund went through anyway.

7.A: Says: write a summary file; start two new sessions that each read it.
7.B: Says: evaluate strategy 1, then strategy 2 afterwards, in the same session.
7.C: Says: clone the session twice — both copies remember the full analysis, then diverge.
7.D: Says: start two blank sessions and re-read the 23 files in each.

8.A: Says: add a second AI that double-checks the first AI's output.
8.B: Says: mark every field required so nothing comes back missing.
8.C: Says: switch to a more capable model.
8.D: Says: add one rule to the prompt: 'if the article doesn't state it, return null.'

9.A: Says: make the model attach a confidence score and supporting quote to each skill.
9.B: Says: cap the skill list at 10–20 entries.
9.C: Says: show 2–3 worked examples that demonstrate splitting, only-stated skills, and consistent granularity.
9.D: Says: clean the list afterwards with code (dedupe, filter, merge).

10.A: The case: output SHAPE is wrong (string instead of array) — feedback tells the model exactly what to fix.
10.B: The case: the answer lives in a document the model was never given.
10.C: The case: European number format ('1.234,56') parsed wrong — fixable once pointed out.
10.D: The case: full timestamp returned instead of a date — trivially fixable once pointed out.

11.A: Says: read all 15 files top to bottom, then answer.
11.B: Says: read the largest files first — big must mean important.
11.C: Says: start at the base class and interface, follow the structure down to the invalidation logic.
11.D: Says: grep for 'invalidate', read only those snippets.

12.A: Says: add a step that first classifies what kind of analysis is wanted, then calls the same vague tool.
12.B: Says: add a mode dropdown (sentiment | entities | summary) to the one tool.
12.C: Says: rewrite the tool's description with clearer instruction examples.
12.D: Says: replace the one do-anything tool with several small tools, each with fixed inputs and outputs.

13.A: Says: pass the draft plus only the NAMES of the sources.
13.B: Says: forward the full 120K+ tokens of accumulated research.
13.C: Says: let the citation agent match claims to sources by similarity, after the fact.
13.D: Says: pass the draft + a map — claim #1 → this URL, this excerpt.

14.A: Says: start over and redo the 2-hour analysis.
14.B: Says: reopen the MOST RECENT session (whatever that is).
14.C: Says: reopen the session by NAME: --resume auth-deep-dive.
14.D: Says: dig through transcript files for the session's ID, then resume by ID.

15.A: Says: show worked examples of extraction from differently-shaped documents (inline citations, bibliographies…).
15.B: Says: when required fields come back empty, automatically retry the request.
15.C: Says: use regex code to find what the model missed and fill the fields in.
15.D: Says: make those fields optional and flag empty records for human review.

16.A: Says: just resume; it'll figure out the renames on its own.
16.B: Says: start a new agent and paste the entire old transcript into it.
16.C: Says: start fresh, seeded with a summary of prior findings.
16.D: Says: resume everything + one note: 'these two functions were renamed while you were paused.'

17.A: Says: throw the session away, rebuild understanding from zero.
17.B: Says: resume and say nothing about the changed files.
17.C: Says: resume + name exactly the 3 changed files so it re-reads only those.
17.D: Says: resume and re-read all 12 files to be safe.

18.A: Says: store findings in a vector DB; on crash, semantic-search it to rebuild state.
18.B: Says: persist the entire conversation log; on crash, replay all of it.
18.C: Says: each agent saves a compact structured report; the coordinator reloads and injects the relevant ones.
18.D: Says: each agent keeps its own private state file and restores itself independently.

19.A: Says: extract each field with its own separate API call.
19.B: Says: extract raw, then normalize the formats in code afterwards.
19.C: Says: run the extraction 3–5 times and keep the majority answer per field.
19.D: Says: one call with a strict schema + explicit format rules in the prompt ('prices: 12.00, dates: YYYY-MM-DD').

20.A: Says: the coordinator LLM reads each query and decides which agents (if any) to involve.
20.B: Says: two fixed lanes — simple queries take the fast lane, complex ones get the full pipeline.
20.C: Says: write pattern-matching routing rules mapping query types to pipelines.
20.D: Says: train a separate ML classifier to route queries.

21.A: Says: tune the confidence thresholds before launch.
21.B: Says: pilot on a small slice of live traffic and watch what happens.
21.C: Says: break the 97% down BY document type — verify no segment is secretly failing.
21.D: Says: survey the ops team about which errors hurt most.

22.A: Says: the model writes a complete plan up front, then executes it step by step.
22.B: Says: developers hard-code a decision tree: if X happens, call tool Y.
22.C: Says: an orchestration layer (software) decides which tool runs next.
22.D: Says: each tool result is appended to the conversation; the model reads it and freely decides the next move.

23.A: Says: when sources go missing, search the web again to reconstruct where claims came from.
23.B: Says: force summaries to keep bracketed citations inside the prose.
23.C: Says: make summaries structured — text in one field, source list (title/URL/date) in another.
23.D: Says: stop summarizing entirely; pass full raw content through every stage.

24.A: Says: errors come back structured: retryable true/false + a customer-friendly explanation, straight from the tool.
24.B: Says: add prompt examples teaching the model to interpret each error string.
24.C: Says: the tool itself silently retries transient failures before responding.
24.D: Says: add a check_refund_eligibility tool that must run before every refund attempt.

25.A: Says: delete the generic Write tool so the model is forced onto the new ones.
25.B: Says: rewrite each tool's description — what it does, when it beats sed/text-manipulation, its inputs and outputs.
25.C: Says: bolt on an external intent classifier that routes to the right tool.
25.D: Says: accept it; model preference is fine.

26.A: Says: convert everything into flowing paragraphs.
26.B: Says: invent one universal intermediate format everything converts into first.
26.C: Says: instruct the synthesis step — tables stay tables, narrative stays prose, filings get quoted with citations.

27.A: Says: wipe the context (/clear) and start the physics task clean.
27.B: Says: distill the rendering discoveries into a note; hand a fresh subagent that note + the new task.
27.C: Says: run the physics task in a separate subagent and manually combine the answers at the end.
27.D: Says: stay in the tired context and just prompt harder.

28.A: Says: skip batch; process each contract in real time at full price.
28.B: Says: submit a batch every 6 hours (worst case 6 + 24 = 30h — exactly the SLA).
28.C: Says: submit every 4 hours (worst case 28h — two hours of cushion).
28.D: Says: submit one batch at end of business day.

29.A: Says: add a citation-resolution agent that mines the logs afterwards to reattach sources.
29.B: Says: every conclusion travels with its source IDs as a data field, preserved at every stage.
29.C: Says: prefix sentences with source tags like [SRC-2] inside the text.
29.D: Says: match claims back to sources by semantic similarity after the fact.

30.A: Says: subagent runs happen, but their context arrives broken (forwarding misconfigured).
30.B: Says: the coordinator's prompt doesn't tell it that subagents exist.
30.C: Says: the subagent descriptions got truncated by context limits.
30.D: Says: the coordinator was never GIVEN the Task tool — it can talk about delegating but cannot do it.

31.A: Says: follow a preset checklist regardless of what each step reveals.
31.B: Says: investigate step by step — each finding decides the next subtask.
31.C: Says: launch four parallel agents, one per architecture layer, merge results.
31.D: Says: map everything first, write the complete plan, then explore.

32.A: Says: after each tool call, rewrite the result as a short prose summary.
32.B: Says: keep only the return-relevant fields (items, dates, window, status); drop the other ~35.
32.C: Says: store results in a vector database and retrieve pieces on demand.
32.D: Says: do nothing; context windows are big enough.

33.A: Says: rewrite the system prompt with stronger, more prominent wording about the $500 rule.
33.B: Says: the refund tool itself validates and rejects amounts ≥ $500.
33.C: Says: a code hook intercepts every refund call — ≥ $500 gets blocked AND escalated, no model discretion.
33.D: Says: add few-shot examples of the model behaving correctly near the limit.

34.A: Says: set temperature to 0 so output is deterministic.
34.B: Says: switch to a more capable model.
34.C: Says: mark materials as a required field.
34.D: Says: show 2–3 examples of messy input → one clean standardized materials format.

35.A: Says: build a classifier that picks detailed vs loose instructions per task type.
35.B: Says: keep the script but add fallback branches ('if insufficient, try X, then Y').
35.C: Says: drop all instructions; just say 'research X.'
35.D: Says: state the GOAL + a quality bar (coverage, diversity, recency); the agent chooses its own path.

36.A: Says: find every file that imports the library and read each one.
36.B: Says: check the documentation for known usages.
36.C: Says: first list every name the function is exported AS (all aliases), then grep for each name.
36.D: Says: grep for the original name, calculateTax, and update those hits.

37.A: Says: the system prompt needs an instruction to remember user details.
37.B: Says: some tool is wiping the model's memory between turns.
37.C: Says: the app isn't re-sending earlier messages — the API itself remembers NOTHING between calls.
37.D: Says: Claude keeps only two turns by default; raise that setting.

38.A: Says: write notes to a scratchpad, /clear, then selectively re-read key files.
38.B: Says: spawn subagents for specific questions ('find the test files', 'trace the refund path'); keep only their findings.
38.C: Says: summarize the learning so far and rely on that summary alone from now on.
38.D: Says: stop reading whole files; work from grep snippets only.

39.A: Says: fork yesterday's session twice; each branch designs one approach with full memory.
39.B: Says: open fresh sessions and manually re-explain yesterday's context.
39.C: Says: design approach 1, then approach 2, back-to-back in one session.
39.D: Says: fresh sessions seeded with a summary of yesterday's analysis.

40.A: Says: force the model to pick the closest of the 4 types, no matter what.
40.B: Says: every time a new type appears, add it to the enum list.
40.C: Says: drop the enum; property_type becomes free text.
40.D: Says: add 'other' to the enum + a detail field that holds the actual label.

41.A: Says: filter out findings below a confidence threshold before synthesis.
41.B: Says: only keep findings confirmed by at least two independent sources.
41.C: Says: attach probability scores and average conflicting values together.
41.D: Says: structure reports into 'established' vs 'contested', keeping each source's own wording about uncertainty.

42.A: Says: the MCP server silently retries all failures itself before responding.
42.B: Says: add a second tool (analyze_error) the agent calls to diagnose what an error meant.
42.C: Says: teach the model with examples how to react to 'Operation failed.'
42.D: Says: errors return structured metadata — {category: permission, retryable: false, description}.

43.A: Says: the coordinator failed to paste the research findings into the synthesis prompt.
43.B: Says: the cause is that agents can't read each other's conversation histories.
43.C: Says: findings were passed but got truncated by context limits.
43.D: Says: the agents need a shared API connection to auto-share context.

44.A: Says: build a hierarchy — agents spawn sub-agents that spawn sub-sub-agents.
44.B: Says: build a real message-queue system that distributes precedent jobs.
44.C: Says: the coordinator itself fans precedent batches out to parallel subagents and merges their reports.
44.D: Says: the analysis agent spawns its own helpers whenever it decides to.

45.A: Says: keep the 80K handoff but enable prompt caching so it's cheaper.
45.B: Says: skip the handoff — the coordinator already holds the findings and summarizes them itself.
45.C: Says: pre-generate summaries at several detail levels, just in case one is requested.
45.D: Says: give the summary agent a retrieval tool to fetch pieces of the coordinator's context on demand.

46.A: Says: split the analyzer into three tools (each with an equally thin description).
46.B: Says: add routing rules to the system prompt: 'for dependency questions, use dependency_analyzer.'
46.C: Says: remove Grep so it can't be chosen.
46.D: Says: rewrite the description — returns the full import graph, transitive deps, cycles; and when to prefer it over Grep.

47.A: Says: persist the full conversation to a database and give the human a reference ID to look up.
47.B: Says: forward only the customer's original message to the human.
47.C: Says: escalate WITH a package — customer details, order info, what was found, what approval is needed.
47.D: Says: attempt the refund anyway and let the system's rejection trigger the review.

48.A: Says: keep only the most recent 30 turns in context (sliding window).
48.B: Says: compress resolved issues into narrative summaries; keep the active issue verbatim.
48.C: Says: maintain a structured record per issue (order IDs, amounts, statuses) that persists through the whole conversation.
48.D: Says: store nothing — re-call the lookup tools whenever an old issue comes up.

49.A: Says: ask one more clarifying question and try to solve it first.
49.B: Says: run a quick order lookup, then decide whether to escalate.
49.C: Says: explain what the agent CAN do; escalate only if the customer insists again.
49.D: Says: escalate right now, attaching the context that they've explained the issue twice already.

50.A: Says: hand over the customer's verbatim complaint plus relevant transcript excerpts.
50.B: Says: hand over just the diagnosis and amount: 'duplicate charge, $847.'
50.C: Says: hand over customer ID + root cause + amount + recommended action.
50.D: Says: hand over a long summary of all 25+ turns.

51.A: Says: give Edit a 30+ line block as the match target so it's unique.
51.B: Says: append the helper at the END of the file instead.
51.C: Says: Read the whole file, insert the helper at the right spot in memory, Write the file back.
51.D: Says: use replace_all on the repeating docstring pattern.

52.A: Says: switch to a model with a larger context window.
52.B: Says: the agent writes findings to a notes file and RE-READS it instead of remembering.
52.C: Says: pre-summarize every file up front and work only from the summaries.
52.D: Says: wipe the context every 15 minutes to keep it fresh.

53.A: Says: auto-escalate after any 3 consecutive failed tool calls.
53.B: Says: hard-code a rules engine; remove the model's judgment entirely.
53.C: Says: give the model clear criteria (asks for a human / needs a policy exception / no progress) and let it judge.
53.D: Says: escalate when message sentiment or punctuation (!!!) crosses a threshold.
